doc.title: Jonathan Scales interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 23, 2025

title: Composing from the emotion to be expressed
summary: He starts with what he wants listeners to feel, then chooses notes, rather than attaching emotion to ideas afterwards.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah that’s definitely one way of going about things you know. I definitely find – just to dabble into it just slightly – I definitely find that when people are writing music a lot of times people say they start with the melody or they start with a chord progression or they start with a rhythm and they start with, you know, they sat down and they came up with something and then that sparked something. I always write music from like a reverse, from like an inverted space from that. Like I first start with what is it that I want to express. We’re making art, you know? I’m thinking what is it that I want to express and what is it that I want the audience to feel and what is trying to be conveyed here. Now that is going to dictate what the notes are, the structures, blah-blah-blah. And I do feel like a lot of times – and this is not good or bad, this is not right or wrong – but I feel like a lot of people when they make music they come up with ideas first and then they retroactively attach an emotion to that. You see what I’m saying?

They retroactively attach an emotion to the thing they randomly created as opposed to what is it that I want people to feel from this, and what is the best combination of notes, rhythms, phrases, styles, articulations, dynamics, all of this stuff that I have in my toolbox to best bring to life the idea that I’m trying to convey. You see what I’m saying?
